coherence.reasons: Both run the same clean chain: quantified bridge, three driver deep-dives, sized plan, sequencing, risks, decisions. X is tighter, but its governing thought promises "~3%" while its base case is 2.8% and needs stretch levers. X also books a shrink gain from restoring routines in the leanest stores without costing the hours, while cutting 8% of hours in the other half. Y's governing thought (2.9–3.1%) matches its bridge, and its labor reinvestment ties the shrink and labor levers together. Against that, Y's slide 3 is a process detour about its own working hypothesis, and it compares a Wave 1 run-rate and an FY2028 low case with a covenant that is tested on FY2026. These roughly cancel.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the answer key's preferred type of plan (R1 with a targeted labor element) and reject the management draft. Y weighs alternatives more fully: an options table covers the draft, the plan without the three board-vote stores, the plan plus exiting home delivery, and growing e-commerce, each with operating income, margin, one-time cost and constraint fit. Y also sizes the trade-offs inside its levers: a 1% volume loss from cutting promotions, up to $2M reinvested in everyday prices near ValuMart, and 1% of chain hours put back into fresh and receiving. It adds a low/base/high range, stage gates and a contingency tranche. X's trade-offs are acknowledged but thinner: promotions are valued with no volume loss, the labor cut is a heavier 8% in half the stores, and one-time costs beyond the $7.5M are left uncosted, so the $25M cap is not really tested. X is more prudent in absorbing the full wage rise and in giving an in-year FY2026 covenant view.

evidence.reasons: Both reproduce the key calculations correctly: the margin bridge, the gross-margin drivers, the −$10.4M e-commerce drag, the rebuttal of the 6.1% claim, the fee-test saving of about $2.5M and the $6.6M store-exit gain. Y uses the evidence slightly more fully: it notes the category team's comparison is not controlled for location, uses the Q3≈Q4 shrink gap to justify where hours can be trimmed, and nets a volume loss against the promotion saving. But Y introduces more unsupported numbers: the vendor-funding sizing rests on a speculative reading of the 14-point gap, half the wage rise is assumed recovered in prices despite worsening price perception, and most one-time costs are invented allowances. Its $10M shrink giveback is also an aggressive time-series extrapolation, though all of these are flagged. X invents less and treats the wage rise cautiously, but calls its case "cautious" while assuming no volume loss on promotions, and leaves most one-time costs unquantified. Net, the two are about even.

revision.reasons: Both revise management's wage hypothesis in the way the answer key expects. Each shows labor is about 13% of the decline, splits the wage effect from the hours effect, links the hours reductions to shrink, and quantifies why the draft plan falls short (X: about 1.5%, range 1.0–2.0%; Y: 0.9–1.7%). Both keep the part the evidence supports: wages are a real pressure, the 2027 rise is absorbed, and a targeted trim is retained. Y's slide 3 tests the team's own starting hypothesis rather than management's, but it still tests "wages are not the main cause" and asks the board to withdraw the blanket cut. X is equally clear in replacing the draft plan. No meaningful difference.

overall.reasons: The diagnoses are essentially identical and both correct. Y would serve the CEO better at the board because it gives a fuller decision package: an explicit comparison of five options including the delivery-exit fallback, a costed one-time budget against the $25M cap, a low/base/high range, stage gates and contingency, and levers that net out second-order effects such as promotion volume loss and labor reinvestment. X is leaner, more conservative on wages and more direct on the FY2026 covenant, but it leaves the capital budget largely uncosted and relies on stretch levers and a no-volume-loss promotion assumption to approach the target. Y's weak points are its vendor-funding sizing and the assumed half recovery of the wage rise in prices, both flagged.
